title: Alcohol Misuse: AUDIT Screening and Brief Intervention

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with possible hazardous or harmful drinking: Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) scoring and intervention zones, and inpatient withdrawal treatment with benzodiazepines and thiamine, using the WHO AUDIT and two NHS hospital protocols.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: NICE CG115 and CG100 could not be opened; withdrawal doses are from two NHS hospital protocols (Greater Glasgow and Clyde for mental health wards and Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals) and have not been compared with a national formulary or a Saudi protocol.
The chlordiazepoxide fixed-dose schedule tables (NNUH pages 16 to 17) were not extracted in full; only the stat dose, first-24-hour cumulative limit and symptom-triggered maximum were read.
Relapse-prevention drugs (acamprosate, naltrexone, disulfiram) were not covered by any source opened.
Pregnancy: the NNUH guideline excludes pregnancy; no pregnancy advice was obtained.
The GGC diazepam day 4 maximum is printed as 10 mg, below the scheduled 15 mg doses, and looks like a typographical error; it is not reproduced.
Symptoms and signs are general clinical features and are not all listed in the extracts opened.
Alcohol possession and treatment in Saudi Arabia are subject to local law and hospital policy; no Saudi guideline was opened.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

pathophysiology.summary: The protocols opened treat alcohol withdrawal with a fixed or symptom-triggered benzodiazepine regime and monitor with observations or a withdrawal scale. Wernicke's encephalopathy is a medical emergency in a patient with alcohol misuse and is treated with parenteral thiamine. Liver impairment changes the benzodiazepine choice to oxazepam. AUDIT scores guide whether education, simple advice, brief counselling or specialist referral is appropriate.
keyMechanisms: The protocols opened treat alcohol withdrawal with a fixed or symptom-triggered benzodiazepine regime and monitor with observations or a withdrawal scale.

redFlags: Acute confusion, ataxia, reduced consciousness, unexplained hypotension with hypothermia, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, or memory disturbance: treat as Wernicke's encephalopathy.
Severe dependence needing doses above the standard limits.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Confusion, ataxia, eye signs; urgent parenteral thiamine.

clinicalManagement.title: Screen with AUDIT
actions: Score the 10 items and apply the zone-based intervention.
Use the clinical override to move up a level when questions 4, 5, 6, 9 or 10 are high.

clinicalManagement.title: Check for Wernicke's encephalopathy
actions: Give parenteral thiamine if confusion, ataxia or eye signs are present.

clinicalManagement.title: Start withdrawal treatment
actions: Diazepam fixed regime for adults; oxazepam for liver impairment; chlordiazepoxide per the NNUH symptom-triggered approach.
Monitor vital signs every 4 hours; watch for over-sedation.

clinicalManagement.title: Replace thiamine
actions: Parenteral thiamine then oral thiamine; continue while problem drinking continues.

regimens.indication: Alcohol withdrawal on mental health wards (fixed regime)
regimens.dose: Day 1 to 2: 20 mg four times a day (as needed 20 mg); day 3 to 4: 15 mg four times a day; day 5: 15/10/10/15 mg; day 6: 10 mg four times a day; day 7: 10/5/5/10 mg; day 8: 5 mg four times a day; day 9: 5 mg three times; day 10: 5 mg twice; day 11: 5 mg once
regimens.frequency: Four times a day on scheduled days
adjustments: Doses above 50 mg a day only for severe dependence with close monitoring; above 80 mg a day only for very severe dependence and never in older people or liver impairment.
Older adults: separate 10-day regime starting 10 mg four times a day.
monitoring: Blood pressure, pulse and temperature every 4 hours; over-sedation.
contraindications: Respiratory disease and pregnancy cautions are not given in the source.
Diazepam injection is contraindicated in severe liver impairment (NNUH).

regimens.indication: Alcohol withdrawal with known liver impairment
regimens.dose: Day 1: 40 mg four times a day (as needed 40 mg); day 2: 40/30/40/40 mg; day 3: 30/30/30/40 mg; day 4: 30/20/30/30 mg; day 5: 20/20/20/30 mg; day 6: 20/10/20/20 mg; day 7: 10/10/10/20 mg; day 8: 10 mg four times a day; day 9: 10 mg twice; day 10: 10 mg once
regimens.frequency: Four times a day on scheduled days
adjustments: Doses above 90 mg a day only for severe dependence; above 120 mg a day only for very severe dependence.
contraindications: Contraindications are not listed in the extract opened.

regimens.indication: Alcohol withdrawal on general wards (symptom-triggered or fixed)
regimens.dose: Initial stat dose 30 mg; fixed schedules start at 20, 30 or 40 mg four times a day on days 1 and 2 by alcohol units; cumulative regular plus as-needed dose up to 200 mg in the first 24 hours
regimens.frequency: Four times a day (fixed) or as needed with CIWA-Ar score of 10 or more, then review in one hour
regimens.duration: Fixed schedule tables on pp. 16 to 17 (not extracted); maximum 200 mg a day if symptom triggered
adjustments: Consider oxazepam in older adults or significant liver damage; in decompensated liver disease use symptom-triggered dosing with lowest possible as-needed doses.
Lorazepam 2 mg sublingual (1 mg if over 65) when oral treatment is not possible.
monitoring: Observations at least every 8 hours for 72 hours then daily; CIWA-Ar one to four hourly by score.
contraindications: Haloperidol, if needed, is contraindicated in CNS depression, coma or congenital long QT syndrome.

regimens.indication: Prevention and treatment of Wernicke's encephalopathy (inpatient, high-dose)
regimens.genericName: Pabrinex (thiamine and B vitamins), two pairs of ampoules
regimens.route: Intravenous infusion over 30 minutes in 100 mL sodium chloride 0.9%
regimens.duration: 3 to 5 days or until clinically settled
adjustments: GGC uses one pair intramuscularly daily as a 5-day course; oral thiamine follows.
monitoring: Facilities for treating anaphylaxis available; very low anaphylaxis risk cited (about 1 in 1 million intravenous).
contraindications: Known allergy to any component or previous reaction.

regimens.frequency: NNUH three times a day; GGC four times a day
regimens.duration: NNUH: 3 to 6 months after abstinence or indefinitely if heavy drinking continues, 28 days on discharge; GGC: indefinitely while problem drinking continues
adjustments: Consider multivitamin with trace elements if diet is poor (GGC).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Score 16 to 19: simple advice plus brief counselling and continued monitoring.
Score 20 to 40: refer to a specialist for diagnostic evaluation and treatment.

teaching.scope: Adult with possible hazardous or harmful drinking: Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) scoring and intervention zones, and inpatient withdrawal treatment with benzodiazepines and thiamine, using the WHO AUDIT and two NHS hospital protocols.
learningObjectives: Score AUDIT and match intervention to zone.
Treat withdrawal with benzodiazepines and thiamine.
pitfalls: Using benzodiazepines at standard doses in liver impairment.
keyPoints: AUDIT zone 8 to 15 simple advice; 20 or more refer.
Pabrinex IV three times a day for 3 to 5 days in NNUH.
